When an effect hook injects a DOM element with a known ID via `insertAdjacentHTML` or similar, first check `document.getElementById(id)` and skip insertion if the element already exists, preventing duplicates when multiple component instances mount. In the corresponding cleanup, retrieve the element with `getElementById` and guard the removal with an existence check (e.g., `element?.parentNode?.removeChild(element)`) rather than a non-null assertion, so the cleanup does not throw if the element was already removed by other code.

When a helper called inside a `useEffect` body returns a cleanup/teardown function, capture that return value and invoke it inside the `useEffect`'s own cleanup callback; silently discarding it means teardown logic (e.g., restoring a DOM style property) never runs when the effect re-fires or the component unmounts.

Do not parse a CSS `filter` property value by splitting on whitespace—filter functions such as `drop-shadow(2px 2px 4px black)` contain spaces within their arguments and will be fragmented incorrectly. Instead, save the entire original filter string before modification and restore it verbatim in cleanup, or use a regex that matches complete filter function tokens.

TypeScript triple-slash directives (`/// <reference types="..." />`) must not be followed by a trailing semicolon; the semicolon causes TypeScript to treat the line as an ordinary comment rather than a directive.

When writing a dynamic `import()` expression for a third-party package, verify whether the target symbol is a default export or a named export before deciding on import syntax. CommonJS-compiled packages frequently expose their main class only as a default export; destructuring `{ SymbolName }` from such a module yields `undefined` at runtime. If the package uses a default export, access it as `(await import('pkg')).default`.

Before adding `import type { SomeName }` from a package (external or internal), confirm that `SomeName` is actually present in that package's published type declarations or exports. For external packages, check `.d.ts` files or re-exports. For internal renderer types (e.g., a framework type alias in a renderer's `types.ts`), verify the type is defined and exported. If the type does not exist, define it locally—for example via `ConstructorParameters<typeof ThePlugin>[0]` or a hand-written interface—or reuse an existing type rather than importing a non-existent named type.

When writing GitHub Actions conditions to detect or skip fork PRs, use `github.event.pull_request.head.repo.fork != true` rather than comparing `github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository`. The `full_name` comparison can silently misbehave when `head.repo` is null (e.g., the originating fork was later deleted), while the boolean `fork` property is the purpose-built, null-safe alternative. This pattern is already established in `trigger-circle-ci-workflow.yml` and should be used consistently across all workflow files.
Unit tests for URL-building functions must include cases for special characters in parameter values (e.g., `=`, `&`, `;`, `:` within a value) to verify that encoding is applied correctly end-to-end.

Do not use `rel="canonical"` on `<a>` elements—the canonical link type is only valid on `<link>` tags in the document `<head>` for SEO canonicalization. On anchor tags, omit `rel` entirely for internal navigation links and use `rel="noreferrer"` only for external links that open in a new tab.

Components that render `href` attributes derived from current navigation state (e.g., the active settings-tab path in the sidebar Menu) must subscribe to routing state changes so the `href` value stays accurate throughout the session. A static `href` computed at initial render silently becomes stale after navigation and can mislead users and crawlers.

Avoid redeclaring, shadowing, or confusingly naming a local variable the same as an imported symbol or a binding already in scope from an enclosing destructuring. Before introducing a new `const`, verify no binding with the same name exists in the current or outer scope; before returning an expression, verify each identifier resolves to the intended binding. This is a recurring pitfall in `manager-api` modules that destructure `store.getState()`.

When implementing paired sibling-navigation helpers in `manager-api/modules/stories.ts` (e.g., `findSiblingComponent` and `findSiblingStory`), both helpers must derive the active ref context from the same source. Prefer reading `refId` from the fully resolved story/item object (e.g., `story.refId`) rather than reading it directly from raw state, so both helpers behave consistently when navigating across refs.

When reading a feature flag from `global.FEATURES` inside manager components (e.g., `Sidebar.tsx`, `GuidePage.tsx`), always use optional chaining together with a `!== false` guard—`global.FEATURES?.flagName !== false`—so that the flag defaults to its enabled state (`true`) when `FEATURES` is undefined, which can occur in tests and stories.

Preset functions that invoke external analysis utilities (e.g., docgen extraction, file reads) and utilities that parse stringified function source (e.g., regex-based source parsing in `mount-utils.ts`) must wrap those calls in `try/catch` and return a safe fallback (e.g., `null`) on failure so that exceptions do not propagate and crash preset loading or story rendering.

Always use `getProjectRoot()` from `storybook/internal/common` when computing paths relative to the project root; do not use `process.cwd()`, which may differ from the project root when the Node process is launched from a subdirectory.

When a result object uses a boolean `success` discriminator alongside optional fields, model it as a proper TypeScript discriminated union (`{ success: true; fieldA: string } | { success: false; error?: string }`) so the compiler narrows required fields within branches and non-null assertions are unnecessary.

When generating mock or dummy values for compound types (arrays, tuples), iterate over each element's `SBType` and call the value generator recursively rather than hardcoding a single scalar for all elements; e.g., a `[number, string]` tuple should produce `[42, '']`, not `['mock string', 'mock string']`.

When a type-name allowlist guards renderer-specific handling at one layer of the type-mapping pipeline (e.g., array-element processing in `extractDocgenInfo`), keep it in sync with all type-name mappings defined at higher or peer layers; any name handled by the top-level mapping (e.g., `JSX.Element`, `ComponentType`) must also appear in downstream allowlists that gate element-level handling.

When reading ArgType metadata such as the `required` flag, access it from the `ArgType` entry itself (e.g., `argType.required`), not from the nested `SBType` object; `SBType` carries no `required` field, so reading from there will always yield `undefined`.

When writing functions that sanitize or generate JavaScript identifier names by stripping invalid characters (e.g., `sanitizeIdentifier` in `csf-tools/vitest-plugin/component-transformer.ts`), also verify that the resulting string does not start with a digit—JS identifiers cannot begin with `[0-9]`. If the sanitized value starts with a digit, prefix it with `_` (or another safe character) before returning it, in addition to any existing empty-string fallback.

In test files, the module path passed to `vi.mock()` must exactly match the module path used in `import` statements in the file under test; a mismatch silently leaves the real implementation in place and causes tests to call production code instead of the mock.

Catch blocks must not silently swallow errors; never use empty `catch {}` blocks, including in test lifecycle hooks (e.g., Storybook `afterEach` hooks in `test-annotations.ts`). Even for non-critical or best-effort code paths, log the caught error at minimum at debug level (using `logger.debug` from `storybook/internal/node-logger` on the server side) or forward it to a reporting API (e.g., `reporting.addReport()`) before continuing or returning, so failures remain visible during troubleshooting.

All return paths of a function must return a consistent type; an early-exit guard that returns `undefined` (or nothing) when every other path returns a typed value is a bug—return the same type on all branches.
Guard-and-early-return checks must be placed before the work they are meant to skip; do not call an expensive function and then check afterward whether you should have called it.
Use `import { join } from 'path'` (platform-aware) rather than `import { join } from 'path/posix'` for paths passed to file-system operations or external processes, to avoid breakage on Windows.
When a computed value (such as an elapsed duration) is calculated before a conditional return, use that computed value in the returned payload rather than a hardcoded fallback (e.g., `0`).

External sub-process invocations (e.g., spawning `vitest` or other CLI tools via `executeCommand`) must be bounded by a timeout; use `Promise.race` with a rejection timer or a timeout option on the execution API to prevent indefinite hanging.

Always wrap `JSON.parse` calls that parse data from external sources (files, process output, network responses) in a try-catch block, and return a descriptive error object on parse failure rather than letting the exception propagate as an unhandled error.
Remove duplicate entries from exported array constants; duplicates waste memory, can produce unexpected behaviour in callers that iterate or check membership, and indicate a copy-paste mistake.

When a `useEffect` registers window-level event listeners (mousemove, mouseup, etc.) inside a nested callback (e.g., an onStart handler spawned from a mousedown), the effect's cleanup function must also remove those nested window listeners. Only cleaning up the directly-registered listeners leaves orphaned handlers if the component unmounts mid-interaction.

Utility functions that cycle or index into a collection must handle the empty-collection edge case explicitly. If the stated return type is non-nullable (e.g., `string`) but `Object.keys(map).length` could be 0, add an early guard that returns a safe sentinel or throws a descriptive error rather than silently returning `undefined`.

Do not use `.replace('px', '')` to extract numeric values from CSS dimension strings. This silently produces wrong results for non-pixel units (`%`, `em`, `rem`, `vw`, `vh`). Use `parseFloat()` or a regex that strips any trailing unit characters (e.g., `/[a-z%]+$/i`) so all unit types are handled correctly.

When renaming a DOM element's `id` (or the selector used to query it), search the entire codebase for every consumer of the old ID—`querySelector`/`querySelectorAll` calls, `href` skip-link anchors, `aria-controls`/`aria-labelledby` attributes, and tests—and update them all in the same commit. Partial migrations silently break features such as skip navigation.

Every `<input>` element must have an associated `<label>` element linked via a stable ID. Use `useId` (e.g., from `@react-aria/utils`) to generate a unique ID and pass it to both the `htmlFor` attribute of the label and the `id` attribute of the input. Unlabeled inputs are a WCAG 2.1 Level A violation and will be flagged by accessibility audits.

When a toolbar or canvas control's state is externally locked (e.g., overridden by story globals or parameters), every interactive control that would mutate that state—buttons, text inputs, select dropdowns—must be visually disabled (`disabled` attribute or `aria-disabled`) and reject interaction. A control that accepts input but silently does nothing is both a misleading UX and an accessibility failure.

When a preset-selection dropdown coexists with freeform value inputs (e.g., a viewport picker alongside width/height fields), the dropdown must expose a distinct 'Custom' or equivalent state that activates whenever the user overrides the preset values. Without it, selecting or opening the dropdown can silently discard the user's custom values.

Toolbar addons and canvas-level UI that are only meaningful in story mode must gate their rendering on `viewMode`. Rendering addon controls in docs mode (or other non-story contexts) where they have no effect produces confusing, non-functional UI.

When writing a regex to validate that a parsed token is a JavaScript identifier, use a complete pattern that constrains every character—e.g., `/^[a-z_$][0-9a-z_$]*$/i`—rather than a partial check that only inspects the first and last characters; partial checks silently allow strings like `foo-bar` or `a#b` to pass.

Before inserting any variable into a `new RegExp(...)` constructor, escape all regex metacharacters in the variable first (e.g., `v.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, '\\$&')`), even when the variable is derived from a trusted internal source such as stringified function source; skipping this step risks regex injection, parse errors, and ReDoS exposure.

When using a regex pattern like `{([^}]+)}` to capture content inside braces, be aware that it will prematurely terminate at the first `}` when the content itself contains nested braces (e.g., default values such as `{ a = { nested: true } }`); either use a balanced-brace algorithm, restrict usage to contexts where nesting is impossible, or add a JSDoc/inline comment explicitly documenting the known limitation.

When extracting the body of a stringified function, match from the first `{` to the *last* `}` using a greedy pattern such as `/^[^(]*\([^)]*\)[^{]*\{([\s\S]*)\}\s*$/`; a pattern that terminates at the first `}` will silently truncate the body of any function whose body contains nested `{}` blocks (object literals, control-flow statements, etc.).

Avoid `forEach(async (item) => { ... })` when sequential execution is intended; this pattern fires all iterations concurrently and silently discards the returned Promises, causing interleaved output and no ordering or error-propagation guarantees. Use `for (const item of list) { await ... }` instead, and ensure any accompanying code comments accurately reflect whether execution is sequential or parallel.

When assigning to a nested property on an externally-sourced options or config object (e.g., `programmaticOptions.env.bugfixes = true`), always guard that the intermediate object exists before assigning into it—e.g., `obj.prop = obj.prop || {};`—rather than assuming the caller populated it. Check how the same file already handles analogous nested-property access and follow the same defensive pattern for consistency.

When a test file imports a module that the corresponding production/runtime code also imports, ensure both use the same import form (default import vs. named import). A mismatch can silently mask ESM/CJS export incompatibilities that only surface in production, and makes the test a poor proxy for real-world behavior.

Switch `case` clauses that declare local variables (`const` or `let`) must wrap their entire body in a `{ }` block to comply with Biome's `noSwitchDeclarations` rule and prevent the variable from being accessed by other cases.

When CSS dimensions are computed using a reciprocal scale factor (e.g., `(1 / scale) * 100%` paired with `transform: scale(scale)`) or any division-based arithmetic, guard against zero, negative, and non-finite values at both the input-validation layer and defensively at the computation site (e.g., `Math.max(scale, 0.001)`) to prevent `Infinity`, `NaN`, or negative CSS values from corrupting the layout. Do not apply a numeric scale multiplier directly to percentage-unit strings—percentages are relative, not absolute; restrict numeric scaling to absolute-unit values (px, em, rem) or pass percentage units through unmodified.

When using `forwardRef<T, P>`, the generic `T` must exactly match the object returned by `useImperativeHandle`. If the ref should expose a custom interface (e.g., `{ select: () => void }`), return that interface from the factory function rather than forwarding the raw DOM element; or change the generic to the actual DOM element type if direct element access is intended.

When guarding on the result of `String.prototype.search()`, use `index >= 0` (or `index !== -1`), not `index > 0`. The value `0` is a valid match position at the start of the string, so `> 0` silently skips that case. The same applies to `indexOf()`.

Avoid `Array.prototype.findLast()` (ES2023) and `Array.prototype.at()` (ES2022) unless the project's browserslist or build pipeline explicitly targets environments that ship these methods natively. Use ES2020-compatible alternatives: `[...arr].reverse().find(pred)` instead of `arr.findLast(pred)`, and `arr[arr.length - 1]` instead of `arr.at(-1)`.

In numeric input handlers, detect `NaN` with an explicit `Number.isNaN(value)` check and early `return` rather than relying on numeric comparison operators. Because `NaN >= 0` evaluates to `false`, guards that rely on numeric comparisons silently swallow NaN without making the intent clear, leading to subtle downstream bugs.

When spawning child processes with `spawn()`, always attach both an `'error'` listener and a `'close'` listener. Without an `'error'` handler, a spawn failure (bad interpreter path, missing file, permission denied) emits an unhandled `error` event that crashes the Node process. The `'error'` handler should log via `logger.error` without rethrowing. When spawning shell scripts, use the bare interpreter name `'sh'` rather than an absolute path like `'/bin/sh'`; POSIX does not require `sh` to live in `/bin/`, and Node.js resolves bare command names through `$PATH`.

Use optional chaining (`?.`) consistently throughout a property access chain on a potentially-null value; avoid mixing `value?.prop` with `value['key']` (a non-optional bracket access) on the same nullable object—use `value?.['key']` for bracket access on nullable references.

Never call `.sort()` directly on a module-level constant array (e.g., `CATEGORIZATION_RULES.sort(...)`); this mutates the shared reference on every invocation. Pre-compute a sorted copy at module initialization (`const SORTED_RULES = [...CATEGORIZATION_RULES].sort(...)`) and reference that constant instead.

When querying child nodes to call element-only methods like `getBoundingClientRect()` or `getComputedStyle()`, use `firstElementChild` / `children` (which return only `Element` nodes) rather than `firstChild` / `childNodes`; the latter can return `Text` or `Comment` nodes, which will throw on element-specific API calls.

When checking CSS `opacity` for visibility, compare numerically (`parseFloat(style.opacity) > 0`) rather than via string equality (`style.opacity !== '0'`); browsers may return `'0.0'` or `'0.00'`, which string comparison incorrectly treats as visible.

When running multiple independent fallible async operations with `Promise.all`, wrap each item in a per-item try-catch (or use `Promise.allSettled`) so that one failing operation does not reject the entire batch and crash the caller; fall back to a safe default on individual errors.

Every value of an enum or category constant set must have an explicit handler in any switch/case or mapping lookup that processes it; do not allow defined values (including error/unknown categories) to fall through to a generic default when a specific, actionable description or behavior exists.

Captured error variables in `catch` blocks (e.g., `const errorMessage = error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error)`) must be used—either logged, included in the returned error payload, or forwarded to a reporting API. Leaving the variable unused silently discards diagnostic information.

When spawning child processes with a custom `env` object, always spread `process.env` first (`{ ...process.env, CUSTOM_VAR: value }`) to inherit `PATH`, `NODE_ENV`, and other required variables; providing only custom keys without the parent environment will break the spawned process.

React hooks (including `useRef`, `useState`, `useEffect`, and any custom hooks) must be called unconditionally at the top level of a component function, before any early returns or conditional branches. If a hook call appears after an early return, move it above that return. This is required by React's Rules of Hooks.

When changing the rendered element type of a component (e.g., `<div>` to `<nav>`, `<section>` to `<header>`), update every associated `useRef<T>` generic parameter to match the new element type (e.g., `useRef<HTMLDivElement>` → `useRef<HTMLElement>`) so the ref stays type-safe.

Before replacing a CSS-hide pattern (`display: none`, `visibility: hidden`, `hidden` attribute, or a wrapper that renders-but-conceals) with conditional mounting/unmounting, verify that the hidden component's internal state does not need to survive the hide/show cycle. Unmounting destroys state; CSS hiding preserves it.

When inserting new entries into a CLI flags array that will be passed to `executeCommand` (or a similar subprocess helper), check whether the array includes a `--` argument-separator and insert the new flags in the correct position relative to it. Flags pushed before `--` are consumed by the invoking command; flags pushed after `--` are forwarded to the subprocess. Misplacing a flag on the wrong side of the separator silently changes which process receives it.

When building a string array whose entries must match keys in a TypeScript interface or object literal (e.g., a `hardcodedShortcuts` or `fixedShortcuts` list used for filtering), verify the exact case-sensitive spelling of every entry against the target keys. A casing mismatch compiles without error but silently fails to match at runtime.

The keyboard shortcut key string rendered in the UI (e.g., `['alt', '+']`) must match the string registered with the shortcut system (e.g., `['alt', '=']`). On US keyboards `+` and `=` share a physical key but differ as string values; mismatched strings mean the visual hint describes a different key combination than the one that actually fires the action.

After calling a computation utility (e.g., `getComponentComplexity()`), validate the result with `Number.isFinite(result)` before using it in sorting, averaging, or other arithmetic; edge-case parsing errors or division by zero can produce `NaN`/`Infinity`, which corrupts downstream calculations.

When building argument arrays for subprocess or command execution (e.g., `executeCommand`, `spawn`), always push CLI flags and their values as separate array elements (e.g., `parts.push('-p', String(port))`) rather than as a single combined string (e.g., `parts.push(`-p ${port}`)``). A combined string is passed as one argument token, causing the flag to be silently ignored or misinterpreted by the target CLI.

When calling `api.setAddonShortcut`, every registration must use a unique `actionName`; reusing an existing `actionName` silently overrides the previously registered shortcut. If a logical action needs multiple keyboard shortcuts, use distinct `actionName` values (e.g., `zoomIn` and `zoomInAlt`)—each will appear as a separate entry in the keyboard shortcuts configuration table.

When changing error handling from throwing to silent skipping of non-conforming items (e.g., non-factory exports in `CsfFile.ts`), ensure tests cover all plausible shapes that could be accidentally dropped—including raw function components (`() => <Component />`) and plain story objects (`{ args: {} }`)—not just trivial helpers. Evaluate whether a `logger.warn()` should be emitted when items are silently skipped, so users receive diagnostic feedback instead of silently missing content.

When clamping a dimension against a minimum size constant while a zoom/scale factor is in play, clamp in logical (unscaled) units first and then multiply by scale: `Math.max(MIN, logicalValue) * scale`. Do not clamp after scaling (`Math.max(MIN, logicalValue * scale)`), because that applies the minimum in physical pixels—at non-1× zoom the displayed logical value will fall below the intended minimum.

When the CLI AST-transform layer (e.g., `eslintPlugin.ts`) matches a `CallExpression` by its callee identifier name, always resolve the identifier back to its `ImportDeclaration` and verify it originates from the expected source package before mutating the AST. Matching only the local binding name is insufficient—a user config may import an identically-named function from a different package, which must be left untouched.

When writing a regex to match or strip a specific literal sentinel/token string (e.g., the `$SNIP` marker from `cleanPaths` in `code/core/src/telemetry/sanitize.ts`), verify that no quantifier (`?`, `*`, `+`) inadvertently makes any character optional. For example, `/\$SNIP?/g` matches both `$SNI` and `$SNIP`; use `/\$SNIP/g` to match only the full intended token.

When reviewing changes to the component detection heuristic in `component-transformer.ts`, verify whether the logic correctly scopes what counts as a 'component' export. Flag any new code paths that risk generating tests for non-renderable exports (e.g., HOC factory functions), and ensure the inline comment noting future refinement is updated if the heuristic is tightened.

When building an absolute-positioned overlay (e.g., a suffix mask `div`) that must visually align with text inside a styled `<input>`, offset the overlay's `left` to match the input's horizontal padding as defined in the shared `Form/styles.ts`. To stay in sync without hardcoding, extract the padding value into a shared constant or CSS variable referenced by both the input style definition and the overlay.

When writing boolean conditions that combine multiple equality checks with `||`, ensure every disjunct is a complete comparison expression—`a === b || c` where `c` is a truthy variable is NOT equivalent to `a === b || a === c`. Always write out the full comparison on each side of `||` (and `&&`) to avoid silent operator-precedence bugs.

When adding non-editable informational elements (e.g., unit or suffix labels) adjacent to an `<input>`, give the element a stable `id` using `useId` from `@react-aria/utils` and link it to the input via `aria-describedby={suffixId}` so screen readers announce the supplementary context when the field receives focus.
Maintainability and Readability: When destructuring an array to skip leading elements, use an empty slot (e.g., `const [, value] = arr`) rather than a throwaway `_` variable. Named-but-unused `_`-prefixed bindings can trigger the project's `@typescript-eslint/naming-convention` lint rule. Default values can be applied in the same pattern (e.g., `const [, value = []] = arr`).

When migration docs or other documentation links to external code examples, consider whether to link to the final file on the default branch or to a PR diff. Link to a PR diff when the purpose is to show readers what changes to make; if so, ensure the surrounding prose makes it explicit so readers know to follow the diff pattern.

Use meaningful, descriptive `id` and `className` values on DOM elements; avoid placeholder names (e.g., `figure-out-id`) and legacy or ambiguous class names that no longer clearly describe the element's role.

Extract repeated or non-obvious magic values (pixel sizes, durations, numeric defaults) into named module-level constants or CSS variables. Reference these constants everywhere they appear—including inside callbacks and nested functions—so a single change propagates everywhere. Do not inline raw literals when a named constant already exists in the same file.

Use specific, user-facing text for initial or default UI states rather than vague placeholders; a label that clearly communicates what has not yet occurred is easier to understand at a glance than a generic 'not yet' phrase.

When using non-obvious encodings in source code (e.g., a two-digit hex suffix for alpha opacity like `#aabbcc22`), add a brief inline comment explaining the encoding so future readers do not have to decode it.

On framework-specific documentation pages, verify that all prose references to the framework name (builder, renderer, etc.) match the page's actual subject. Copy-pasting from a sibling page commonly introduces incorrect framework name references.

The opening sentence of the Install section in `docs/get-started/frameworks/*.mdx` pages should follow the canonical phrasing: "To install Storybook in an existing [Framework] project, run this command in your project's root directory."

When editing framework documentation pages, check for and remove any content—migration callouts, configuration notes, or version-specific guidance—that applies only to Storybook major versions that are no longer supported or relevant to current users.

Keep PRs strictly scoped to their stated objective. Verify that every changed file is traceable to the PR's purpose; flag any unrelated changes and request extraction into a separate, focused pull request with its own description, tests, and documentation. In dependency-upgrade PRs specifically, flag any source or configuration changes that go beyond package manifest updates and mechanical API-migration fixes (e.g., renamed types, updated call signatures); ask the author to confirm each such change is intentional and explain why it is part of the upgrade.

In Vitest test files, place mock setup (`vi.mocked(...)`, `vi.spyOn(...)`, `mockImplementationOnce`, `mockResolvedValueOnce`, etc.) in `beforeEach` blocks rather than inline within individual `it`/`test` bodies. Use nested `describe` blocks to scope test-specific configurations. Call `vi.clearAllMocks()` in `beforeEach` or `afterEach` to prevent cross-test state leakage.

When adding non-obvious filtering or defensive logic that compensates for stale persisted state (e.g., `shortcutKeys` entries from localStorage never registered in the current session), include an inline comment explaining *why* the filtering is required—not just what it does.

Add JSDoc (`/** */` block comments, not `/* */`) to every exported utility function in framework, shared, and preset packages (e.g., under `code/frameworks/`, `code/core/`), including `internal_*` and `experimental_*` preset API functions. Document each function's purpose, each parameter, the full range of return values—including graceful-failure paths (e.g., 'returns `false` when the version string cannot be coerced by semver')—and stability status for preset APIs. Use `/** */` syntax so IDE hover tooltips are populated. Mark deprecated exports with the `@deprecated` JSDoc tag naming the replacement, e.g., `@deprecated Use api.getStoryHrefs from storybook/manager-api`. When types or interfaces in `scripts/ci/` map directly to external framework constructs (e.g., CircleCI step types, executor shapes), include a link to the relevant official documentation in the JSDoc description.

When an API's configuration already constrains its callback arguments (e.g., `MutationObserver` with `attributeFilter`, or a typed event handler), do not add redundant `forEach` loops, `if` checks, or other guards that re-verify the guaranteed constraint; the extra code adds noise without safety.

Add explanatory inline or JSDoc comments to code that implements non-obvious workarounds (e.g., browser quirks, framework-specific issues like React.StrictMode, cross-frame communication). The comment should describe the problem being solved, the specific runtime conditions or environment under which it occurs, and where applicable link to the relevant spec issue or browser bug, so future maintainers can reason about scope and continued necessity.

Reference shared internal constants (e.g., channel event names from `storybook/internal/core-events`, `STORYBOOK_FN_PLACEHOLDER`) by their exported named identifier everywhere they appear—production code, test assertions, and JSDoc comments—rather than hardcoding their string value. Never use inline magic strings for event names in `emit`/`on` calls.

Name event constants (e.g., in `core-events`) after the semantic purpose or behavioral contract they establish for consumers—what they should do or what state has changed—rather than the low-level browser mechanism that triggers them (e.g., prefer `FOCUS_TRAP_CHANGE` over `INERT_ATTRIBUTE_CHANGED`).

When editing MIGRATION.md, verify that no explanatory paragraph or sentence is accidentally duplicated within or across sections; each breaking-change or deprecation notice should appear exactly once.

When documenting or writing `yarn task` commands (in READMEs, instructions, AI-assistant guidance, etc.), always include the `--start-from` flag (e.g., `--start-from auto`) to prevent the CLI from entering interactive mode and blocking in non-interactive contexts such as CI or agent sessions. Use `yarn task` as the primary documented command form (the project's canonical task-runner wrapper); if raw `yarn nx` equivalents are shown, present them as alternatives alongside the `yarn task` form.

When attaching module-private metadata to objects (e.g., indentation style on a parsed `package.json`), define a module-level `Symbol('description')` constant (not `Symbol.for()`, which creates globally-shared symbols) and use it as the property key. Compute and attach such metadata at parse/load time so downstream writers can access it without a redundant file read. Add a brief inline comment noting that `JSON.stringify` silently omits symbol-keyed properties, as this serialization behavior is not universally known.

Avoid combining an existence check with a side-effecting operation in a single conditional expression. Separate them into distinct statements—first check, then act—so each step is independently readable and the side effect cannot be accidentally triggered as part of predicate evaluation.

When writing a comment that explains why an error is suppressed or treated as non-fatal, name the exact error type (e.g., `AbortError`) rather than using vague language like 'any errors' with a parenthetical example. Precision helps future maintainers know whether new error types should also be covered.

When introducing a custom helper type in a documentation snippet (e.g., under `docs/_snippets/`, to extend component props with additional story args), add a short comment directly above the type explaining its purpose and clearly stating whether it is optional for readers implementing the pattern in their own code.

When adding a callout or warning about a cross-cutting behavior (e.g., a builder quirk that affects build output), verify the note appears on every related documentation page—both the configuration API reference page and the corresponding integration or how-to guide—so the caveat is not buried in only one location.

When Storybook documentation recommends setting a Vite configuration option, specify that the setting must be applied through the `viteFinal` hook in `.storybook/main.ts` rather than referencing the Vite option in isolation; include an inline code snippet (e.g., `async viteFinal(config) { config.publicDir = false; return config; }`) or a link to Storybook's Vite builder documentation so readers know exactly where and how to apply the change.

When a utility is copied into a package because the original cannot be imported across a package boundary (e.g., the preview-to-manager boundary in addon-docs), add a `/** */` JSDoc block on the copy that explains: why it is duplicated, how it differs from the canonical version (e.g., only returns a preview URL rather than `{ managerHref, previewHref }`), and where the canonical version lives.

When calling `stringify` from `picoquery` in manager-api or router code, align the serialization options with the canonical usage in `code/core/src/router/utils.ts` (at minimum `nesting: true` and `nestingSyntax: 'js'`); document any intentional deviation from those defaults.

Do not leave test cases permanently disabled with `test.skip()` without an accompanying tracking issue or TODO that includes a resolution plan; error and exception branches (e.g., catch blocks and cross-origin fallback paths) must have dedicated test coverage.

When extracting a component ID from a story ID, do not split on `'--'` manually (e.g., `storyId.split('--')[0]`). Check whether `storybook/internal/csf` already provides a helper for story/component ID manipulation and use it instead.

Storybook tag strings such as `'autodocs'`, `'test'`, `'dev'`, `'manifest'`, `'attached-mdx'`, `'unattached-mdx'`, `'play-fn'`, and `'test-fn'` must be referenced via the canonical `Tag` object (defined in `code/core/src/shared/constants/tags.ts`, re-exported from `storybook/internal/core-server` for server/node code and from `storybook/manager-api` for manager/browser code). Raw string literals for these values are not acceptable anywhere in the codebase, including renderer packages such as `code/renderers/react/`.

`code/core/src/manager/globals/exports.ts` is auto-generated by `code/core/scripts/generate-source-files.ts`. Do not manually add or remove entries from this file; instead run the generator script so it discovers new exports (e.g., from `storybook/manager-api/index.ts`) automatically. Manual edits will be overwritten the next time the generator runs.

Avoid CSS selector overrides in a parent/wrapper styled component that target internals of a child component (e.g., `table { backgroundColor: ... }` inside a wrapper div). Components should accept styling customization only through explicit APIs such as props or a `className` prop. If the child component lacks the necessary API for context-specific styling, extend the child component with that API rather than reaching into it with an ancestor selector. When a styling fix is correct for all usages of a component (not just one specific consumer), apply the change in the component's own definition rather than as a context-specific override in a single consumer.

When adding or modifying entries in `sandbox-templates.ts` to enable a Storybook configuration option for CI coverage, check whether the option is supported by both Webpack and Vite builders; if it is, add sandbox entries for both builder types rather than only one. When setting a modification flag on a sandbox template (e.g., `useCsfFactory: true`), apply the same flag to all builder variants (Vite, Webpack, RsBuild) of the same renderer unless there is a documented technical reason they must differ. If only one builder supports the option, add a comment explaining why the other is omitted.

When rendering a Radix-UI–style polymorphic component (such as `ActionList.Action`) as an anchor element, use the `asChild` pattern—pass an `<a>` element as a JSX child—rather than supplying an `as='a'` prop. This is the established polymorphism convention throughout this codebase.

When adding a new feature flag to the `StorybookConfigRaw` features interface (in `code/core/src/types/modules/core-common.ts`), choose user-facing, discoverable names rather than internal technical jargon. Prefer terminology users are likely to search for in documentation (e.g., 'onboarding') and include a surface-area scope prefix (e.g., 'sidebar') when the flag controls behaviour in a specific part of the UI. The flag name, its default in the preset (`common-preset.ts`), and all usage sites must all use the same identifier.

Preset hook functions intended solely for internal Storybook-to-Storybook consumption must use the `internal_` prefix (e.g., `internal_getArgTypesData`); reserve the `experimental_` prefix for APIs that are deliberately surfaced to end users.

Preset hook functions should follow the chainable accumulator pattern `(input: T, options: Options) => T` so they compose correctly in preset chains; if an internal hook must have a different input/output shape, document the deviation explicitly.

Renderer-specific preset hook functions that require file-system access should use async FS APIs and be declared `async`; since `core-server` will consume these hooks uniformly across all renderers, an async contract must be established from the start to keep the API consistent.

Do not create two near-identical utility modules that differ only in naming conventions or minor constant values; consolidate them into a single canonical implementation with a clear name and update all call sites, to prevent the two copies from diverging silently.

When adding a new `SBType` variant whose properties must be extensible across multiple renderers or frameworks (e.g., `renderer`), type the property as the open `string` type rather than a closed string-literal union, so new renderers can be integrated without requiring changes to the type definition itself.

Vitest/Jest `describe` block titles must exactly match the name of the function, class, or module under test; stale or incorrect titles produce misleading test-runner output and make failures hard to trace.

Debug log messages must accurately describe and reference the variable actually being logged; if the intent is to log a count or derived value, name it correctly in the message string and pass the right variable. Error return payloads should include the actual captured error message rather than a generic fixed string like `'Failed to find candidates'`.

After refactoring a component to use shared library components (e.g., replacing bespoke styled wrappers with ActionList), remove every import that is no longer referenced in the file. Stale imports create false dependency signals and will trigger lint/compiler warnings.

Do not declare props in a styled component's generic type parameter unless the styling function actually reads and applies them. A prop like `muted?: boolean` that is declared but never used in the styles creates dead API surface: callers pass it expecting an effect, but nothing happens. Either wire the prop into the style logic or remove it from the type.

When replacing a bespoke styled component with a shared design-system component, visually verify in stories that all interactive states (focus ring offset, hover background, active color) still match the surrounding UI. Shared components may default to a different `outline-offset`, `border-radius`, or `background` than what was previously hardcoded, causing subtle visual regressions.

Render purely decorative characters (colons, slashes, separators) via CSS `content` on a `::before`/`::after` pseudo-element rather than as HTML text nodes. Text-node decorators are announced by screen readers and braille displays, adding noise without conveying meaning.

Name component props after what the data semantically *is* (e.g., `aside`, `extra`, `secondary`) rather than where it visually *appears* (e.g., `right`, `trailing`, `end`). Visual layout can change across redesigns, but the underlying data model should not; positional names become misleading after any layout change.

When adding or modifying a utility that parses or detects destructuring patterns in source strings, include unit tests for: (a) properties annotated with inline `//` and block `/* */` comments, (b) trailing-comma and no-trailing-comma variants, (c) renamed/aliased properties (e.g., `{ mount: sbMount }`), and (d) destructuring performed on an object other than the target argument—to surface false positives and false negatives early.

When refactoring code into a conditional branch, audit for dead-code fragments—especially conditional expressions (ternaries, logical operators) that test a variable already known to be a fixed value within that branch. Simplify or remove the expression to reflect the actual runtime state and avoid misleading future readers.

Pure helper functions that do not close over component state (e.g., value parsers, string formatters, unit converters) should be defined at module scope or in a shared utils file rather than inside a component body. Defining them inside a component causes unnecessary re-creation on every render, prevents independent unit testing, and adds noise to the component definition.

Use `<kbd>` elements to wrap individual key names in keyboard-shortcut display components, not `<span>` or `<code>`. The `<kbd>` element has explicit semantic meaning as keyboard input, is announced correctly by assistive technologies, and receives standard browser styling for key labels.

When a list of selectable preset options (e.g., zoom levels, viewport sizes) visually highlights the currently active item, also expose that selection to assistive technology. Append a visually-hidden `(current)` label, set `aria-current`, or include the active state in the element's accessible name so screen reader users know which option is selected without relying solely on visual styling.

When mocking `process.platform` in Vitest tests, use a getter spy—`vi.spyOn(process, 'platform', 'get').mockReturnValue('...')`—rather than `Object.defineProperty`. The getter spy integrates with `vi.restoreAllMocks()` / `vi.resetAllMocks()`, is reliably reversible across Node versions, and prevents the mock from leaking into subsequent tests.

When tests mutate `process.env`, `process.argv`, or spy on `console` methods, save shallow copies of the originals before each test (`const originalEnv = { ...process.env }`) and restore them in `afterEach` or `afterAll` (`process.env = originalEnv`; `.mockRestore()` for console spies). Omitting the teardown causes environment state or suppressed output to leak across tests in the same runner, producing intermittent failures.

When mocking a function in a test, use a return value that matches the actual return type of the real function; avoid `undefined as unknown as ReturnType<typeof fn>` casts that hide a type mismatch—e.g., mock `findConfigFile` (which returns `string | null`) with `null`, not `undefined`.

Negative-only assertions (e.g., `expect(result.code).not.toContain(...)`) in tests should be paired with a positive assertion confirming the code under test actually ran (e.g., that a transform was applied or a generated block is present); without it, a regression that silently produces no output still passes the negative assertion.

Prefer early-return guard clauses (`if (condition) return;`) over wrapping the primary logic in an `if`/`else` block. Early returns reduce nesting and preserve horizontal space for the meaningful code that follows.

When two subtrees in JSX are always rendered in a mutually exclusive, either/or fashion, express this with a ternary (`condition ? <A /> : <B />`) rather than two separate standalone conditionals (`{condition && <A />}` followed by `{!condition && <B />}`). The ternary makes the mutual exclusivity self-evident to readers.

Comments in test files that describe the testing approach (e.g., 'this file tests TypeScript types, so there are no assertions') must accurately reflect the file's actual content. If the file contains both type-level checks and runtime assertions, the comment must acknowledge both. Keep inline test comments synchronized with implementation values they describe—if a threshold or constant changes in the source, update the corresponding test comment to reflect the current value.

Integration test snapshot values for generated data (e.g., dummy arguments) must match what the underlying generator function actually returns; cross-check against unit assertions for the same function to catch mismatches.

Ensure every `it(...)` and `test(...)` call within a test file has a unique, descriptive name. When two tests cover distinct scenarios within the same component category (e.g., plain class components vs. signal-based components), give each a name that unambiguously identifies the differentiating behavior.

When using a depth-limited regex to parse nested structures (instead of a CSS parser or a recursive matcher), add an inline comment that states the nesting depth limit and why the heavier alternative was not chosen. The test suite must include at least one case that exercises the stated maximum depth—relying solely on shallow cases leaves the documented boundary unverified.

When adding or updating GitHub repository links in documentation, verify that each URL actually resolves before merging: check that subdirectory paths within the monorepo are correct (package locations can move between releases), and use `/tree/` rather than `/blob/` when the link target is a directory rather than a file.

When modifying a package-list constant in `code/core/src/shared/utils/ecosystem-identifier.ts` (e.g., `ROUTER_PACKAGES`, `UI_LIBRARY_PACKAGES`, `I18N_PACKAGES`), cross-check the corresponding detection logic in `code/core/src/telemetry/get-has-router-package.ts` and related telemetry files for consistency. If the two lists intentionally diverge in scope or matching strategy (explicit names vs. glob wildcards), add an inline comment explaining the rationale.

In `scripts/ci/utils/constants.ts`, define separate, platform-qualified constants for all root directory paths (e.g., `LINUX_ROOT_DIR` and `WINDOWS_ROOT_DIR`). Never hardcode `/tmp`, `C:\Users\circleci`, or any other OS-specific path string inline in job or helper files; always import and reference the named constant. Executor definitions in `executors.ts` should clearly indicate their target OS in both the name and any path references.

When the `inDevelopment` flag behavior or the process for adding new sandbox templates changes, ensure CONTRIBUTING.md contains an up-to-date, step-by-step guide covering: adding the entry to `sandbox-templates.ts`, setting `inDevelopment: true`, testing locally and on CI, publishing the sandbox via the `generate-sandboxes` pipeline, removing the `inDevelopment` flag before merging, and how to use CI job filtering for iterative local runs (including how dynamic job IDs for sandbox and init-script jobs are constructed).

When composing CI job step arrays in `scripts/ci/` files, use available helper abstractions from `scripts/ci/utils/helpers.ts` (e.g., `verdaccio.publish()`, `workflow.restoreLinux()`, `server.wait()`) instead of inlining equivalent shell commands. Before writing a custom inline step, check whether a helper already exists for that operation.

Add explanatory inline comments for non-obvious conditional logic in CI job definitions—especially in `scripts/ci/sandboxes.ts`—that explain *why* a job is included, excluded, or ordered in a particular way, not just *what* the condition does.

Name CI configuration TypeScript files under `scripts/ci/` based on the category or content of the jobs they define (e.g., `common-jobs.ts`, `sandboxes.ts`, `init-empty.ts`), not based on incidental CircleCI UI group labels or hub names.
Do not commit changes to `yarn.lock` unless actual package dependencies were added, removed, or modified. Revert any unintentional or spurious lock file modifications before requesting review.

Avoid single-letter or terse abbreviated prefixes in local variable names (e.g., `nx`, `ny`, `ux`, `uy`, `vw`, `vh`). Use names that make the variable's role self-evident without needing to decode what the prefix stands for (e.g., `logicalWidth`, `widthUnit`, `scaledHeight`).

When using CSS custom properties to prevent Emotion from generating a new CSS class name on every dynamic value change, the accompanying inline comment should name the specific trigger (e.g., 'on every resize' or 'on every drag update') rather than vague phrasing like 'every possible value', so that the performance rationale is immediately clear to future readers.

When adding a non-obvious boolean or enum prop to a styled component, add or update a JSDoc comment on the component that explains what the prop controls, the behavioral or layout effect it has, and why it exists—particularly when the prop's default behavior is the more common case and the opt-out path is subtle.

When implementing complex multi-step string sanitization or path-transformation utilities (such as `cleanPaths` in `code/core/src/telemetry/sanitize.ts`), add inline comments that explain what each intermediate data structure holds, the intent of each major transformation step, and any non-obvious edge cases being handled (e.g., doubled separators, Windows-style paths). Tests alone are not a substitute for this prose.

When updating existing test assertions to reflect intentionally changed behavior (rather than simply adding new tests or deleting obsolete ones), include a clear explanation—in the PR description or as a comment near the modified assertions—of what the previous expected value was and why the behavior changed. This prevents reviewers from confusing intentional behavioral changes with accidental regressions.
Performance Issue: When filtering a collection based on membership in another collection, pre-compute a `Set` of lookup values outside the loop or `.filter()` callback (e.g., `const ids = new Set(items.map(x => x.id))`) and use `Set.has()` for O(1) membership checks, rather than calling `.some()` or `.includes()` inside the callback, which results in O(n×m) complexity.

When a `useEffect` registers keyboard-shortcut callbacks or other event handlers that close over frequently-changing component state (e.g., the current zoom level), capture that state in a `useRef` and read from the ref inside the callback. This keeps the callback identity stable across renders, prevents the effect from re-running on every state change, and avoids re-registering event handlers on each update.

When defining or modifying CircleCI job resource classes in `scripts/ci/`, verify that each assigned class (`small`, `medium`, `large`, `xlarge`) is genuinely necessary. Prefer smaller resource classes unless there is a concrete reason—such as observed OOM errors or excessive job duration—for a larger one. Call out any `large` or `xlarge` assignments that haven't been justified.
Code Style: Proofread prose in documentation, MIGRATION.md, release-note JSON entries (`docs/versions/`), source-code comments (inline comments, JSDoc blocks, config file comments), and descriptive lists for grammar errors (e.g., possessive 'its' vs. contraction 'it’s', correct plural/verb agreement like 'these props have been removed' not 'these prop has been removed'), common misspellings (e.g., 'superceded' → 'superseded'), stray editing artifacts (e.g., 'Thed' → 'The'), and grammatical parallelism (e.g., use 'well-maintained' rather than bare past participles in a list of adjectives).

In YAML code snippets within documentation (e.g., GitHub Actions workflow examples under `docs/_snippets/`), separate each top-level key (`name`, `on`, `permissions`, `concurrency`, `jobs`, etc.) with a blank line, and add blank lines between major sub-blocks within a job definition (e.g., between `environment` and `steps`) for readability.

In markdown files, bare URLs (e.g., `http://localhost:6006/`) must be wrapped in angle brackets (`<https://example.com>`), markdown link syntax (`[http://localhost:6006/](http://localhost:6006/)`), or enclosed in backtick code formatting. Bare URLs trigger markdownlint rule MD034 (no-bare-urls), which is enforced in this project's linting pipeline.

When adding a TypeScript type alias to a documentation snippet file (e.g., under `docs/_snippets/`), format it using multi-line syntax—one member per line with a trailing semicolon after the closing brace—to stay consistent with the style of existing type definitions in that directory.

In test files (`**/*.test.{ts,tsx,js,jsx}`), all `vi.mock()` calls must include the `{ spy: true }` option per project coding guidelines; this applies to both factory-style and simple mocks, including mocks for `node:` prefixed packages (e.g., `node:fs`, `node:fs/promises`) and internal Storybook packages.

In test assertions, avoid duplicate entries inside `expect.arrayContaining()`; each expected element should appear at most once unless the duplication is intentional and documented with an inline comment explaining why.

Do not use `[^]+` in regular expressions in this codebase; Biome's `noEmptyCharacterClassInRegex` lint rule treats negated empty character classes as errors. Use `[\s\S]` (or `[\\s\\S]` inside a `RegExp` string literal) to match any character including newlines.

Use template literals for log messages that include computed values (e.g., `` `Selected ${candidates.length} files` `` rather than `'candidates files:' + candidates.length`), and log error objects directly (or via `.message`) rather than via template interpolation, which produces `[object Object]`.

Timing-based test assertions (`candidateAnalysisDuration`, `totalRunDuration`, etc.) should use `expect.any(Number)` rather than exact values; even near-instant async operations can produce non-zero durations under load, making exact-value assertions flaky.
In TypeScript files throughout this project, place all type and interface declarations at the top of the file, before any function or variable declarations.
All property and function names in `scripts/ci/` modules must use camelCase; never use snake_case. Flag any snake_case identifiers (e.g., `restore_linux`, `restore_windows`) as naming violations.
